Global Attractors for Hindmarsh-Rose Equations in Neurodynamics

Chi Phan Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of South Florida, Tampa, FL 33620, USA Email address: chi@mail.usf.edu , Yuncheng You Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics, University of South Florida, Tampa, FL 33620, USA Email address: you@mail.usf.edu and Jianzhong Su Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, TX 76019, USA Email address: Su@uta.edu
Date: July 30, 2019
Abstract.

Global dynamics of the diffusive and partly diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations on a three-dimensional bounded domain originated in neurodynamics are investigated in this paper. The existence of global attractors as well as the regularity are proved through various uniform estimates showing the dissipative properties and the asymptotically compact characteristics, especially for the partly diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations by means of the Kolmogorov-Riesz theorem.

Key words and phrases: 
Hindmarsh-Rose equations, neuronal dynamics, global attractor, absorbing property, asymptotic compactness, attractor regularity, partly diffusive system
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 35B41, 35G25, 35K55, 37L30, 92C20; Secondary: 35Q80, 37N25, 60H15

1. Introduction

The Hindmarsh-Rose equations for neuronal spiking-bursting of the intracellular membrane potential observed in experiments was originally proposed in [13, 14]. This mathematical model composed of three coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations has been studied through numerical simulations and mathematical analysis in recent years, cf. [13, 14, 16, 18, 28, 36] and the references therein. It exhibits rich and interesting spatial-temporal bursting patterns, especially chaotic bursting and dynamics, as well as complex bifurcations.

In this work we shall study the global dynamics in terms of the existence of a global attractor for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations, which is a new PDE model in neurodynamics:

(1.1) ∂u∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} =d1​Δ​u+φ⁡(u)+v−w+J,\displaystyle=d_{1}\Delta u+\varphi(u)+v-w+J,\,
(1.2) ∂v∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} =d2​Δ​v+ψ⁡(u)−v,\displaystyle=d_{2}\Delta v+\psi(u)-v,
(1.3) ∂w∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} =d3​Δ​w+q⁡(u−c)−r​w,\displaystyle=d_{3}\Delta w+q(u-c)-rw,

for t>0,x∈Ω⊂ℝnt>0,\;x\in\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} (n≤3n\leq 3), where Ω\Omega is a bounded domain with locally Lipschitz continuous boundary. The nonlinear terms

(1.4) φ⁡(u)=a​u2−b​u3,andψ⁡(u)=α−β​u2.\varphi(u)=au^{2}-bu^{3},\quad\text{and}\quad\psi(u)=\alpha-\beta u^{2}.

The inject current JJ is treated as a constant, but it can be a given function J​(x)∈L2​(Ω)J(x)\in L^{2}(\Omega) and all the results in this paper remain valid.

In this system (1.1)-(1.3), the variable u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) refers to the membrane electric potential of a neuronal cell, the variable v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) represents the transport rate of the ions of sodium and potassium through the fast ion channels and is called the spiking variable, while the variables w⁡(t,x)w(t,x) represents the transport rate across the neuronal cell membrane through slow channels of calcium and other ions correlated to the bursting phenomenon and is called the bursting variable.

All the involved parameters are positive constants except c(=uR)∈ℝc\,(=u_{R})\in\mathbb{R}, which is a reference value of the membrane potential of a neuron cell. In the original model of ODE [36], a set of the typical parameters are

J=3.281,r=0.0021,S=4.0,q=r​S,c=−1.6,\displaystyle J=3.281,\;\;r=0.0021,\;\;S=4.0,\;\;q=rS,\;\;c=-1.6,
φ⁡(s)=3.0​s2−s3,ψ⁡(s)=1.0−5.0​s2.\displaystyle\varphi(s)=3.0s^{2}-s^{3},\;\;\psi(s)=1.0-5.0s^{2}.

We impose the Neumann boundary conditions for the three components,

(1.5) ∂u∂ν​(t,x)=0,∂v∂ν​(t,x)=0,∂w∂ν​(t,x)=0,t>0,x∈∂Ω,\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\;\;\frac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\;\;\frac{\partial w}{\partial\nu}(t,x)=0,\quad t>0,\;x\in\partial\Omega,

and the initial conditions

(1.6) u⁡(0,x)=u0​(x),v⁡(0,x)=v0​(x),w⁡(0,x)=w0​(x),x∈Ω.u(0,x)=u_{0}(x),\;v(0,x)=v_{0}(x),\;w(0,x)=w_{0}(x),\quad x\in\Omega.

We shall also consider the partly diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations

(1.7) ∂u∂t=d1​Δ​u+φ⁡(u)+v−w+J,∂v∂t=ψ⁡(u)−v,∂w∂t=q⁡(u−c)−r​w\begin{split}\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}&=d_{1}\Delta u+\varphi(u)+v-w+J,\\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial t}&=\psi(u)-v,\\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial t}&=q(u-c)-rw\end{split}

and

(1.8) ∂u∂t=d1​Δ​u+φ⁡(u)+v−w+J,∂v∂t=d2​Δ​v+ψ⁡(u)−v,∂w∂t=q⁡(u−c)−r​w.\begin{split}\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}&=d_{1}\Delta u+\varphi(u)+v-w+J,\\ \frac{\partial v}{\partial t}&=d_{2}\Delta v+\psi(u)-v,\\ \frac{\partial w}{\partial t}&=q(u-c)-rw.\end{split}

In neuronal dynamics, the partly diffusive models (1.7) or (1.8) is more commonly interesting, since the ions currents may or may not diffuse.

1.1. The Hindmarsh-Rose Model in ODE

In 1982-1984, J.L. Hindmarsh and R.M. Rose developed the mathematical model to describe neuronal dynamics:

(1.9) d​ud​t=a​u2−b​u3+v−w+J,d​vd​t=α−β​u2−v,d​wd​t=q⁡(u−uR)−r​w.\begin{split}\frac{du}{dt}&=au^{2}-bu^{3}+v-w+J,\\ \frac{dv}{dt}&=\alpha-\beta u^{2}-v,\\ \frac{dw}{dt}&=q(u-u_{R})-rw.\end{split}

This neuron model was motivated by the discovery of neuronal cells in the pond snail Lymnaea which generated a burst after being depolarized by a short current pulse. This model characterizes the phenomena of synaptic bursting and especially chaotic bursting in a three-dimensional (u,v,w)(u,v,w) space, which incorporates a third variable representing a slow current that hyperpolarizes the neuronal cell.

Neuronal signals are short electrical pulses called spike or action potential. Neurons often exhibit bursts of alternating phases of rapid firing spikes and then quiescence. Bursting constitutes a mechanism to modulate and set the pace for brain functionalities and to communicate signals with the neighbor neurons. Bursting behaviors and patterns occur in a variety of bio-systems such as pituitary melanotropic gland, thalamic neurons, respiratory pacemaker neurons, and insulin-secreting pancreatic β\beta-cells, cf. [2, 3, 6, 14].

The mathematical analysis mainly using bifurcations together with numerical simulations of several models in ODEs on bursting behavior has been studied by many authors, cf. [1, 9, 10, 18, 19, 28, 30, 32, 36]. The more interesting study is on the behavior of neurons coupling and synchronization [8, 10, 23, 26].

Neurons communicate and coordinate actions through synapses or diffusive coupling called gap junction in neuroscience. Synaptic coupling of neurons has to reach certain threshold for release of quantal vesicles and synchronization [7, 22, 25].

The chaotic coupling exhibited in the simulations and analysis of this Hindmarsh-Rose model in ordinary differential equations shows more rapid synchronization and more effective regularization of neurons due to lower threshold than the synaptic coupling [30, 36]. It was rigorously proved in [28, 36] that chaotic bursting solutions can be quickly synchronized and regularized when the coupling strength is large enough to topologically change the bifurcation diagram based on this Hindmarsh-Rose model, but the dynamics of chaotic bursting is highly complex.

It is known that Hodgkin-Huxley equations [15] (1952) provided a four-dimensional model for the dynamics of membrane potential taking into account of the sodium, potassium as well as leak ions current. It is a highly nonlinear system if without simplification assumptions. FitzHugh-Nagumo equations [11] (1961-1962) derived a two-dimensional model for an excitable neuron with the membrane potential and the current variable. This model admits an exquisite phase plane analysis showing spikes excited by supra-threshold input pulses and sustained periodic spiking with refractory period, but due to the 2D nature FitzHugh-Nagumo equations exclude any chaotic solutions and chaotic dynamics so that no chaotic bursting can be generated.

It has been indicated by research that the Hindmarsh-Rose model in ODE causes lower the neuron firing threshold. More importantly, this Hindmarsh-Rose model allows varying interspike-interval. Therefore, this 3D model is a suitable choice for the investigation of both the regular bursting and the chaotic bursting when the parameters vary. The study of dynamical properties of the Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.9) as a neuron model exposes to a wide range of applications in neuroscience.

The rest of Section 1 is the formulation of the system (1.1)-(1.3) and provides basic concepts and results in the theory of global dynamics. In Section 2 we shall conduct uniform estimates to show the absorbing properties of the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow in L2​pL^{2p} spaces for 1≤p≤31\leq p\leq 3. In Section 3, the main result on the existence of global attractor for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose system is proved. Section 4 will show the regularity and structure of the global attractor. Finally, in Section 5 we shall prove the asymptotic compactness of the two partly diffusive systems (1.7) and (1.8) by means of the Kolmogorov-Riesz theorem and the existence of global attractors.

1.2. Formulation and Preliminaries

Neuron is a specialized biological cell in the brain and the central nervous system. In general, neurons have four parts: the central cell body containing the nucleus and intracellular organelles, the dendrites, the axon, and the terminals. The dendrites are the short branches near the nucleus receiving incoming signals of voltage pulse. The axon is a long branch to propagate outgoing signals. The nerve terminals communicate these pulse signals to other neurons.

Neurons are immersed in aqueous chemical solutions consisting of different diffusive ions electrically charged. The voltage and concentration-dependent conductances of these various ions can give rise to different neural behavior. As pointed out in [17], neuron is a distributed dynamical system.

From physical and mathematical point of view, it is meaningful and useful to consider the Hindmarsh-Rose model in partial differential equations with the spatial variables xx involved. Here in the abstract extent, we shall study the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.1)-(1.3) and the partly diffusive models (1.7) and (1.8) in a bounded domain of space ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} and focus on the global dynamics of the solutions.

We start with formulation of the aforementioned initial-boundary value problem of (1.1)–(1.6) into an abstract evolutionary equation. Define the Hilbert space H=[L2​(Ω)]3=L2​(Ω,ℝ3)H=[L^{2}(\Omega)]^{3}=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) and the Sobolev space E=[H1​(Ω)]3=H1​(Ω,ℝ3)E=[H^{1}(\Omega)]^{3}=H^{1}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}). The norm and inner-product of HH or L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) will be denoted by ∥⋅∥\|\,\cdot\,\| and ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\,\cdot,\cdot\,\rangle, respectively. The norm of EE will be denoted by ∥⋅∥E\|\,\cdot\,\|_{E}. The norm of Lp​(Ω)L^{p}(\Omega) or Lp​(Ω,ℝ3)L^{p}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) will be dented by ∥⋅∥Lp\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}} if p≠2p\neq 2. We use |⋅||\,\cdot\,| to denote a vector norm in a Euclidean space.

The initial-boundary value problem (1.1)–(1.6) is formulated as an initial value problem of the evolutionary equation:

Here the nonnegative self-adjoint operator

where D⁡(A)={g∈H2​(Ω,ℝ3):∂g/∂ν=0}D(A)=\{g\in H^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}):\partial g/\partial\nu=0\} is the generator of an analytic C0C_{0}-semigroup {eA​t}t≥0\{e^{At}\}_{t\geq 0} on the Hilbert space HH due to the Lumer-Phillips theorem [24]. By the fact that H1​(Ω)↪L6​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow L^{6}(\Omega) is a continuous imbedding for space dimension n≤3n\leq 3 and by the Hölder inequality, there is a constant C0>0C_{0}>0 such that

‖φ⁡(u)‖≤C0​‖u‖L63and‖ψ⁡(u)‖≤C0​‖u‖L42for​u∈L6​(Ω).\|\varphi(u)\|\leq C_{0}\|u\|_{L^{6}}^{3}\quad\textup{and}\quad\|\psi(u)\|\leq C_{0}\|u\|_{L^{4}}^{2}\quad\textup{for}\;u\in L^{6}(\Omega).

Therefore, the nonlinear mapping

is a locally Lipschitz continuous mapping. We can simply write column vectors g⁡(t)g(t) as (u⁡(t,⋅),v⁡(t,⋅),w⁡(t,⋅))(u(t,\cdot),v(t,\cdot),w(t,\cdot)) and write g0=(u0,v0,w0)g_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}). Consider the weak solution of this initial value problem (1.10), defined below [4]:

Definition 1.1.

A function g⁡(t,x),(t,x)∈[0,τ]×Ωg(t,x),(t,x)\in[0,\tau]\times\Omega, is called a weak solution to the initial value problem (1.10), if the following conditions are satisfied:

Here (⋅,⋅)(\cdot,\cdot) stands for the dual product of E∗E^{*} and EE, and CwC_{w} stands for the weakly continuous functions valued in HH.

Lemma 1.2.

For any given initial data g0∈Hg_{0}\in H, there exists a unique local weak solution g⁡(t,g0)=(u⁡(t),v⁡(t),w⁡(t)),t∈[0,τ]g(t,g_{0})=(u(t),v(t),w(t)),\,t\in[0,\tau], for some τ>0\tau>0, of the initial value problem (1.10), which satisfies

(1.13) g∈C⁡([0,Tm​a​x),H)∩C1​((0,Tm​a​x),H)∩Ll​o​c2​([0,Tm​a​x),E),g\in C([0,T_{max});H)\cap C^{1}((0,T_{max});H)\cap L_{loc}^{2}([0,T_{max});E),

(1.14) g∈C⁡([t0,Tm​a​x),E)∩C1​((t0,Tm​a​x),H)∩Ll​o​c2​([t0,Tm​a​x),H2​(Ω,ℝ3))g\in C([t_{0},T_{max});E)\cap C^{1}((t_{0},T_{max});H)\cap L_{loc}^{2}([t_{0},T_{max});H^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}))

Proof.

The proof of the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution is made by conducting a priori estimates on the Galerkin approximate solutions of the initial value problem (1.10), these estimates are similar to what we shall present in Section 2, and then by the Lions-Magenes type of weak and weak∗ compactness and convergence argument [4, 24]. The statement of strong solution follows from the parabolic regularity of the evolutionary equations [24, 29]. The details are omitted here. ∎

We do not assume the initial data u0,v0,w0u_{0},v_{0},w_{0}, nor the solutions u⁡(t,x)u(t,x), v⁡(t,x),w⁡(t,x)v(t,x),w(t,x), are nonnegative functions. We do not impose any conditions on any of the positive parameters, nor on the parameter c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} of the equation (1.3), in the proof of all the results in this paper.

Here the goal is to prove the existence and regularity of a global attractor, which will characterize qualitatively the longtime, asymptotic, and global dynamics of all the solution trajectories of this PDE system (1.10) and the hybrid PDE-ODE systems (1.7) and (1.8). As specified in [4, 20, 24, 29] as well as in [33, 34], global attractor is a depository (usually fractal finite-dimensional) of all the permanent regimes including all steady states, periodic or knotted or chaotic orbits, and unstable manifolds for an infinite-dimensional dynamical system. These topics of global dynamic patterns are also important in neural field and neural network theories [5, 10]. For the autocatalytic and Boissonade reaction-diffusion systems [31, 33, 34, 35], it is proved that global attractors exist.

We refer to [4, 20, 24, 29] for the concepts and basic facts in the theory of infinite dimensional dynamical systems, including the few listed here for clarity.

Definition 1.3.

Let {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a semiflow on a Banach space 𝒳\mathscr{X}. A bounded set B0B_{0} of 𝒳\mathscr{X} is called an absorbing set for this semiflow, if for any given bounded subset B⊂𝒳B\subset\mathscr{X} there is a finite time T0≥0T_{0}\geq 0 depending on BB, such that S⁡(t)​B⊂B0S(t)B\subset B_{0} for all t≥T0t\geq T_{0}.

Definition 1.4.

A semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} on a Banach space 𝒳\mathscr{X} is called asymptotically compact if for any bounded sequence {wn}\{w_{n}\} in 𝒳\mathscr{X} and any monotone increasing sequences 0<tn→∞0<t_{n}\to\infty, there exist subsequences {wnk}\{w_{n_{k}}\} of {wn}\{w_{n}\} and {tnk}\{t_{n_{k}}\} of {tn}\{t_{n}\} such that limk→∞S⁡(tnk)​wnk\lim_{k\to\infty}S(t_{n_{k}})w_{n_{k}} exists in 𝒳\mathscr{X}.

Definition 1.5 (Global Attractor).

A set 𝒜\mathscr{A} in a Banach space 𝒳\mathscr{X} is called a global attractor for a semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} on 𝒳\mathscr{X}, if the following two properties are satisfied:

(i) 𝒜\mathscr{A} is a nonempty, compact, and invariant set in the space 𝒳\mathscr{X}.

(ii) 𝒜\mathscr{A} attracts any given bounded set B⊂𝒳B\subset\mathscr{X} in the sense

dist𝒳​(S⁡(t)​B,𝒜)=supx∈Binfy∈𝒜‖S⁡(t)​x−y‖𝒳→0,as​t→∞.\text{dist}_{\mathscr{X}}(S(t)B,\mathscr{A})=\sup_{x\in B}\inf_{y\in\mathscr{A}}\|S(t)x-y\|_{\mathscr{X}}\to 0,\;\;\text{as}\;\;t\to\infty.

The following is the main existing result on the existence of a global attractor.

Proposition 1.6.

[4, 20, 24, 29] Let {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a semiflow on a Banach space 𝒳\mathscr{X}. If the following two conditions are satisfied:

(i) there exists a bounded absorbing set B0⊂𝒳B_{0}\subset\mathscr{X} for {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0}, and

(ii) the semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is asymptotically compact on 𝒳\mathscr{X},

then there exists a global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in 𝒳\mathscr{X} for the semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} and the global attractor is given by

(1.15) 𝒜=⋂τ≥0⋃t≥τ(S⁡(t)​B0)¯.\mathscr{A}=\bigcap_{\tau\geq 0}\;\overline{\bigcup_{t\geq\tau}(S(t)B_{0})}.
Definition 1.7.

Let {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a semiflow on a Banach space XX and let YY be a Banach space which is compactly embedded in XX. Then a set 𝒜⊂Y\mathscr{A}\subset Y is called an (X,Y)(X,Y)-global attractor for this semiflow if the following two conditions are satisfied:

(i) 𝒜\mathscr{A} is a nonempty, compact, and invariant set in YY, and

(ii) 𝒜\mathscr{A} attracts any bounded set BB of XX with respect to the YY-norm.

The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequalities [24, Appendtx B] of interpolation is useful in estimates of solutions of partial differential equations:

where C>0C>0 is a constant, provided that p,q,r≥1,0<θ<1p,q,r\geq 1,0<\theta<1, and

The Young’s inequality in the general form for any nonnegative x,yx,y is

(1.17) xy≤εxp+C(ε,p)yq,1p+1q=1,(p,q≥1),C(ε,p)=ε−q/p.xy\leq\varepsilon x^{p}+C(\varepsilon,p)y^{q},\qquad\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=1,\,(p,q\geq 1),\qquad C(\varepsilon,p)=\varepsilon^{-q/p}.

with ε>0\varepsilon>0 which can be arbitrarily small.

In the sequel, we often write u⁡(t,x),v⁡(t,x),w⁡(t,x)u(t,x),v(t,x),w(t,x) as u⁡(t),v⁡(t),w⁡(t)u(t),v(t),w(t) or even as u,v,wu,v,w for brevity. We shall use CC to denote a generic constant whose value depends on the context. Otherwise, it will be marked as C⁡(ε,D)C(\varepsilon,D) if CC depends on a constant ε\varepsilon and a given set DD or maybe on more quantities.

2. Uniform Estimates and Absorbing Properties

In this section we shall conduct scaled a priori estimates to show that the weak solution of the problem (1.10) exists globally in time and the solution semiflow is dissipative meaning there exists an absorbing set in HH. We shall also prove the absorbing properties in the spaces L4​(Ω,ℝ3)L^{4}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) and L6​(Ω,ℝ3)L^{6}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) for each trajectory, which will play a key role in Section 5 for the study of the partly diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.7) and (1.8).

2.1. Global Existence and Dissipative Property in HH

Theorem 2.1.

For any given initial data g0=(u0,v0,w0)∈Hg_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in H, there exists a unique global weak solution in time, g⁡(t)=(u⁡(t),v⁡(t),w⁡(t)),t∈[0,∞)g(t)=(u(t),v(t),w(t)),\,t\in[0,\infty), of the initial value problem (1.10) for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.1)-(1.3). The weak solution becomes a strong solution on the interval (0,∞)(0,\infty).

Proof.

Taking the L2L^{2} inner-product ⟨(1.1),C1​u​(t)⟩\langle\eqref{ueq},C_{1}u(t)\rangle with an adjustable constant C1>0C_{1}>0 to be determined later, we use the Young’s inequality to get

3. Asymptotic Compactness and Global Attractor

In this section, we show that the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is asymptotically compact and then reach the main result on the existence of a global attractor for this dynamical system associated with the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations.

We now prove the main result on the existence of a global attractor for the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0}.

Theorem 3.2 (The Existence of Global Attractor).

For any positive parameters d1,d2,d3,a,b,α,β,q,r,Jd_{1},d_{2},d_{3},a,b,\alpha,\beta,q,r,J and c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, there exists a global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in the space H=L2​(Ω,ℝ3)H=L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} generated by the weak solutions of the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.10). Moreover, the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} is an (H,E)(H,E)-global attractor.

Proof.

In Theorem 2.2 it has been proved that there is an absorbing set B0∈HB_{0}\in H for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0}. In Theorem 3.1, it is shown that for any given bounded set B⊂HB\subset H,

‖S⁡(t)​g0‖E2≤Q1,for​t≥T1​(B)​and all​g0∈B.\|S(t)g_{0}\|^{2}_{E}\leq Q_{1},\quad\text{for}\;\,t\geq T_{1}(B)\;\,\text{and all}\;\,g_{0}\in B.

This implies that ⋃t≥T1​(B)S⁡(t)​B\bigcup_{t\geq T_{1}(B)}S(t)B is a bounded set in EE, and therefore a precompact set in HH due to the compact embedding E↪HE\hookrightarrow H. Therefore, the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is asymptotically compact in HH. Since the two conditions in Proposition (1.6) are satisfied, we conclude that there exists a global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in the phase space HH for this Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} and

(3.13) 𝒜=⋂τ≥0⋃t≥τ(S⁡(t)​B0)¯.\mathscr{A}=\bigcap_{\tau\geq 0}\;\overline{\bigcup_{t\geq\tau}(S(t)B_{0})}.

Next we prove that this global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} is a bi-space (H,E)(H,E)-global attractor. Actually Theorem 3.1 shows that there is a bounded absorbing set B1⊂EB_{1}\subset E with respect to the EE-norm for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} on HH. Indeed,

(3.14) B1={g∈E:‖g‖E2≤Q1}.B_{1}=\{g\in E:\|g\|^{2}_{E}\leq Q_{1}\}.

Moreover, we can show that the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is asymptotically compact not only in HH but also in the space EE with respect to the EE-norm. Let T>0T>0 be arbitrarily given. For any time sequence {tn}n=1∞,tn→∞\{t_{n}\}^{\infty}_{n=1},\;t_{n}\rightarrow\infty, and any bounded sequence {gn}∈E\{g_{n}\}\in E, there is an integer n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1 such that tn>Tt_{n}>T for all n>n0n>n_{0}. By Theorem 3.1 and the bounded sequence {gn}\{g_{n}\} in EE, we have

{S⁡(tn−T)​gn}n>n0​is bounded set in E.\{S(t_{n}-T)g_{n}\}_{n>n_{0}}\;\text{is bounded set in $E$}.

Since EE is a Hilbert space, there exists an increasing subsequence of integers {ni}i=1∞\{n_{i}\}^{\infty}_{i=1} where ni>n0n_{i}>n_{0} such that the following weak limit exists,

(w)​limi→∞S⁡(tni−T)​gni=g∗∈E.(w)\lim_{i\to\infty}S(t_{n_{i}}-T)g_{n_{i}}=g^{*}\in E.

Since EE is compactly embedded in HH, we can take subsequence of {ni}i=1∞\{n_{i}\}^{\infty}_{i=1} and relabel it as the same as {ni}i=1∞\{n_{i}\}^{\infty}_{i=1}, such that the following strong convergence holds,

(s)​limi→∞S⁡(tni−T)​gni=g∗∈H.(s)\lim_{i\to\infty}S(t_{n_{i}}-T)g_{n_{i}}=g^{*}\in H.

Hence the following strong convergence in EE holds,

limi→∞S⁡(tni)​gni=limi→∞S⁡(T)​S​(tni−T)​gni=S⁡(T)​g∗∈E.\lim_{i\to\infty}S(t_{n_{i}})g_{n_{i}}=\lim_{i\to\infty}S(T)S(t_{n_{i}}-T)g_{n_{i}}=S(T)g^{*}\in E.

This proves that {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is asymptotically compact in EE.

Thus, by Proposition (1.6), there exists a global attractor 𝒜E\mathscr{A}_{E} in EE for the semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0}. Since 𝒜E\mathscr{A}_{E} attracts the set B1B_{1} in the EE-norm and, on the other hand, Theorem 3.1 shows that B1B_{1} absorbs any bounded subset BB of HH, then the global attractor 𝒜E\mathscr{A}_{E} attracts any given bounded set B⊂HB\subset H in EE-norm. Therefore, 𝒜E\mathscr{A}_{E} is an (H,EH,E) global attractor.

Finally, since 𝒜\mathscr{A} is bounded and invariant in HH and in EE, it holds that

𝒜E​attracts​𝒜​in E, so that​𝒜⊂𝒜E,𝒜​attracts​𝒜E​in H, so that​𝒜E⊂𝒜.\begin{split}&\mathscr{A}_{E}\;\text{attracts}\;\mathscr{A}\;\text{in $E$, so that}\;\mathscr{A}\subset\mathscr{A}_{E},\\ &\mathscr{A}\;\text{attracts}\;\mathscr{A}_{E}\;\text{in $H$, so that}\;\mathscr{A}_{E}\subset\mathscr{A}.\end{split}

It concludes that 𝒜\mathscr{A} = 𝒜E\mathscr{A}_{E}. Therefore, the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in HH is an (H,EH,E) global attractor for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow. ∎

4. Regularity Properties and Structure of the Global Attractor

In this section, we shall prove the regularity properties of the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in the spaces L∞​(Ω,ℝ3)L^{\infty}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}) and H2​(Ω,ℝ3)H^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}). And we shall show that the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow is a gradient system so that its global attractor turns out to be the union of the unstable manifolds of all the steady states.

Theorem 4.1.

The global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} in the space HH is a bounded set in L∞​(Ω,ℝ3)L^{\infty}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}). There is a constant C∞>0C_{\infty}>0 such that

(4.1) supg∈𝒜‖g‖L∞≤C∞.\sup_{g\in\mathscr{A}}\,\|g\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C_{\infty}.
Proof.

The analytic C0C_{0}-semigroup {eA​t}t≥0\{e^{At}\}_{t\geq 0} has the regularity property [24] that eA​t:Lp​(Ω)→L∞​(Ω)e^{At}:L^{p}(\Omega)\rightarrow L^{\infty}(\Omega) for p≥1,t>0p\geq 1,t>0, and there is a constant c⁡(p)>0c(p)>0 such that

(4.2) ‖eA​t‖ℒ⁡(Lp,L∞)≤c⁡(p)​t−n2​p,where​n=dim​Ω.\|e^{At}\|_{\mathcal{L}{(L^{p},L^{\infty})}}\leq c(p)\,t^{-\frac{n}{2p}},\quad\text{where}\,\,n=\text{dim}\,\,\Omega.

Since any weak solution of (1.10) as defined is a mild solution [24] and the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} is an invariant set, for any g∈𝒜⊂Eg\in\mathscr{A}\subset E, we have

(4.3) ‖S⁡(t)​g‖L∞≤‖eA​t‖ℒ⁡(L2,L∞)​‖g‖+∫0t‖eA⁡(t−σ)‖(L2,L∞)​‖f⁡(S⁡(σ)​g)−f⁡(S⁡(σ)​0)‖​𝑑σ≤c(2)t−34∥g∥+∫0tc(2)(t−σ)−34L(Q1)(∥S(σ)g∥E+∥S(σ)0∥E)dσ,t>0,\begin{split}&\|S(t)g\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq\|e^{At}\|_{\mathcal{L}{(L^{2},L^{\infty})}}\|g\|+\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{A(t-\sigma)}\|_{(L^{2},L^{\infty})}\|f(S(\sigma)g)-f(S(\sigma)0)\|\,d\sigma\\ &\leq c(2)t^{-\frac{3}{4}}\|g\|+\int_{0}^{t}c(2)(t-\sigma)^{-\frac{3}{4}}L(Q_{1})(\|S(\sigma)g\|_{E}+\|S(\sigma)0\|_{E})\,d\sigma,\quad t>0,\end{split}

where L⁡(Q1)L(Q_{1}) is the Lipschitz constant of the nonlinear map ff restricted on the closed, bounded ball centered at the origin with radius Q1\sqrt{Q_{1}} in EE. The global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} is invariant so that

{S⁡(t)​𝒜:t≥0}⊂B0(⊂H)∩B1(⊂E).\{S(t)\mathscr{A}:t\geq 0\}\subset B_{0}\,(\subset H)\cap B_{1}\,(\subset E).

Then from (4.3) we obtain

(4.4) ‖S⁡(t)​g‖L∞≤c⁡(2)​K1​t−34+∫0tc⁡(2)​L​(Q1)​(Q1+Q2)​(t−σ)−34​𝑑σ=c(2)[K1t−34+4L(Q1)(Q1+Q2)t14],for  0<t≤1,\begin{split}&\|S(t)g\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq c(2)K_{1}t^{-\frac{3}{4}}+\int_{0}^{t}c(2)L(Q_{1})\left(\sqrt{Q_{1}}+\sqrt{Q_{2}}\right)(t-\sigma)^{-\frac{3}{4}}\,d\sigma\\ &\qquad\;\qquad\;=c(2)[K_{1}t^{-\frac{3}{4}}+4L(Q_{1})\left(\sqrt{Q_{1}}+\sqrt{Q_{2}}\right)t^{\frac{1}{4}}],\quad\text{for}\,\,0<t\leq 1,\end{split}

where

Q2=sup0≤σ≤t≤1‖S⁡(σ)​0‖E2.Q_{2}=\sup_{0\leq\sigma\leq t\leq 1}\|S(\sigma)0\|^{2}_{E}.

Take t=1t=1 in (4.4) and get

‖S⁡(1)​g‖L∞≤c⁡(2)​(K1+4​L​(Q1)​(Q1+Q2)),for any​g∈𝒜.\|S(1)g\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq c(2)\left(K_{1}+4L(Q_{1})\left(\sqrt{Q_{1}}+\sqrt{Q_{2}}\right)\right),\quad\text{for any}\;g\in\mathscr{A}.

The invariance of 𝒜\mathscr{A} implies that S⁡(1)​𝒜=𝒜S(1)\mathscr{A}=\mathscr{A}. Therefore, the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} is a bounded subset in L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega). ∎

Theorem 4.2.

The global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in the space HH for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} is a bounded set in H2​(Ω,ℝ3)H^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{R}^{3}).

Proof.

Consider the solution trajectories inside the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A}.

Step 1. Take the L2L^{2} inner-product ⟨(1.1),ut⟩\langle\eqref{ueq},u_{t}\rangle to obtain

where C∞{C_{\infty}} is from (4.1), for the first component u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) of all the solution trajectories in 𝒜\mathscr{A}. Also take the L2L^{2} inner-product ⟨(1.2),vt⟩\langle\eqref{veq},v_{t}\rangle to obtain

for the second component v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) of all the trajectories in 𝒜\mathscr{A}. Then take the L2L^{2} inner-product ⟨(1.3),wt⟩\langle\eqref{weq},w_{t}\rangle to acquire

for the third component w⁡(t,x)w(t,x) of all the trajectories in 𝒜\mathscr{A}.

Summing up the above three estimates we get

Integrating the inequality (4.5) over the time interval [0,1][0,1], we obtain

(4.6) ∫01(‖ut​(s)‖2+‖vt​(s)‖2+‖wt​(s)‖2)​𝑑s≤d1​‖∇u​(0)‖2+d2​‖∇v​(0)‖2+d3​‖∇w​(0)‖2+(a​C∞2+b​C∞3+2​C∞+J)2​|Ω|+(α+β​C∞2+C∞)2​|Ω|+(q​C∞+q​|c|+r​C∞)2​|Ω|≤(d1+d2+d3)​Q1+(a​C∞2+b​C∞3+2​C∞+J)2​|Ω|+(α+β​C∞2+C∞)2​|Ω|+(q​C∞+q​|c|+r​C∞)2​|Ω|.\begin{split}&\int_{0}^{1}(\|u_{t}(s)\|^{2}+\|v_{t}(s)\|^{2}+\|w_{t}(s)\|^{2})\,ds\\[3.0pt] \leq&\;d_{1}\|\nabla u(0)\|^{2}+d_{2}\|\nabla v(0)\|^{2}+d_{3}\|\nabla w(0)\|^{2}\\[4.0pt] &+(a{C_{\infty}}^{2}+b{C_{\infty}}^{3}+2{C_{\infty}}+J)^{2}|\Omega|+(\alpha+\beta{C_{\infty}}^{2}+{C_{\infty}})^{2}|\Omega|\\[4.0pt] &\,+(q{C_{\infty}}+q|c|+r{C_{\infty}})^{2}|\Omega|\\[3.0pt] \leq&\,(d_{1}+d_{2}+d_{3})Q_{1}+(a{C_{\infty}}^{2}+b{C_{\infty}}^{3}+2{C_{\infty}}+J)^{2}|\Omega|\\[3.0pt] &+(\alpha+\beta{C_{\infty}}^{2}+{C_{\infty}})^{2}|\Omega|+(q{C_{\infty}}+q|c|+r{C_{\infty}})^{2}|\Omega|.\end{split}

The dynamical system {S⁡(t)}t≥0\{S(t)\}_{t\geq 0} generated by the diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.10) is a gradient system and the structure of its global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} in H∩EH\cap E is given by

which is the line integral along the trajectory γ⁡(g)⊂ℝ3\gamma(g)\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} over a time interval [0,t][0,t]. Moreover, we can prove that the functional Γ:𝒜(⊂E)→ℝ\Gamma:\mathscr{A}(\subset E)\to\mathbb{R} is continuous. Therefore, by Theorem 10.13 in [20], Γ⁡(g)\Gamma(g) is a continuous Lyapunov functional and the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow a gradient system. Consequently (4.13) is proved. ∎

Remark 1.

The global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow has a finite fractal dimension, which has also been proved indirectly by the existence of an exponential attractor for this semiflow in the space HH. The latter by definition is a set of finite fractal dimension in HH and the global attractor must be a subset of any exponential attractor. That proof has been made in a separate paper by the first two authors but not included here in this paper.

5. Global Attractors for Partly Diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose Equations

In neuronal dynamics, the partly diffusive models (1.7) or (1.8) is more commonly interesting, since the ions currents represented by the variables v⁡(t,x)v(t,x) and w⁡(t,x)w(t,x) may or may not diffuse.

In this section we shall prove the existence of a global attractor for the partly diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations (1.7) and (1.8), respectively. Note that the partly diffusive system (1.7) can be formulated into the evolutionary equation:

(5.1) ∂g∂t=A^g+f^(g),t>0,g(0)=g0=(u0,v0,w0)∈H.\begin{split}&\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}=\hat{A}g+\hat{f}(g),\quad t>0,\\[2.0pt] g&\,(0)=g_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in H.\end{split}

∫Ω|f⁡(x+y)−f⁡(x)|p​𝑑x<εp.\int_{\Omega}|f(x+y)-f(x)|^{p}\,dx<\varepsilon^{p}.

It is a convention that f⁡(x)=0f(x)=0 for x∈ℝn\Ωx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\backslash\Omega.

(5.32) ‖v⁡(t)‖L4≤c~t3/8​‖v0‖+α​t​|Ω|1/2+β​∫0t‖ed2​Δ​(t−s)​u2​(s)‖L4​𝑑s≤c~t3/8​‖v0​‖+α​t​|Ω|1/2+β​∫0t‖ed2​Δ​(t−s)‖ℒ⁡(L2,L4)‖​u2​(s)‖L2​𝑑s=c~t3/8​‖v0‖+α​t​|Ω|1/2+β​∫0t‖ed2​Δ​(t−s)‖ℒ⁡(L2,L4)​‖u⁡(s)‖L42​𝑑s≤c~t3/8​‖v0‖+α​t​|Ω|1/2+β​κ​∫0t‖ed2​Δ​(t−s)‖ℒ⁡(H1)​‖u⁡(s)‖H12​𝑑s≤c~t3/8⫴B⫴+αt|Ω|1/2+β​κd∗​C1(max{C1,1}⫴B⫴2+t(2C2+C12)|Ω|),\begin{split}&\|v(t)\|_{L^{4}}\leq\frac{\widetilde{c}}{t^{3/8}}\,\|v_{0}\|+\alpha t\,|\Omega|^{1/2}+\beta\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{d_{2}\Delta(t-s)}u^{2}(s)\|_{L^{4}}\,ds\\ \leq&\,\frac{\widetilde{c}}{t^{3/8}}\|v_{0}\|+\alpha t\,|\Omega|^{1/2}+\beta\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{d_{2}\Delta(t-s)}\|_{\mathcal{L}(L^{2},L^{4})}\,\|u^{2}(s)\|_{L^{2}}\,ds\\ =&\,\frac{\widetilde{c}}{t^{3/8}}\|v_{0}\|+\alpha t\,|\Omega|^{1/2}+\beta\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{d_{2}\Delta(t-s)}\|_{\mathcal{L}(L^{2},L^{4})}\,\|u(s)\|^{2}_{L^{4}}\,ds\\ \leq&\,\frac{\widetilde{c}}{t^{3/8}}\|v_{0}\|+\alpha t\,|\Omega|^{1/2}+\beta\kappa\int_{0}^{t}\|e^{d_{2}\Delta(t-s)}\|_{\mathcal{L}(H^{1})}\,\|u(s)\|^{2}_{H^{1}}\,ds\\ \leq&\,\frac{\widetilde{c}}{t^{3/8}}\interleave B\interleave+\alpha t\,|\Omega|^{1/2}+\frac{\beta\kappa}{d_{*}C_{1}}\left(\max\{C_{1},1\}\interleave B\interleave^{2}+\,t(2C_{2}+C_{1}^{2})|\Omega|\right),\end{split}

where κ>0\kappa>0 is the H1↪L4H^{1}\hookrightarrow L^{4} embedding constant and ed2​Δ​te^{d_{2}\Delta t} is a contraction semigroup on H1​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega). Take t=1t=1 in (5.32) and we reach a uniform bound

supg0∈B‖v⁡(1)‖L4≤(c~+β​κd∗​C1​(max⁡{C1,1}))⫴B⫴+α​|Ω|1/2+β​κd∗​C1​(2​C2+C12)​|Ω|.\sup_{g_{0}\in B}\|v(1)\|_{L^{4}}\leq\left(\widetilde{c}+\frac{\beta\kappa}{d_{*}C_{1}}\left(\max\{C_{1},1\}\right)\right)\interleave B\interleave+\alpha|\Omega|^{1/2}+\frac{\beta\kappa}{d_{*}C_{1}}(2C_{2}+C_{1}^{2})|\Omega|.

for any given bounded set B⊂HB\subset H and all g0=(u0,v0,w0)∈Bg_{0}=(u_{0},v_{0},w_{0})\in B. Now the bunch of vv-component functions at time t=1t=1 of all these solutions are uniformly bounded in the space L4​(Ω)L^{4}(\Omega). Then the argument in Theorem 2.4 shows that there exists an bounded absorbing set in L4​(Ω)L^{4}(\Omega) for the vv-component functions of all these solutions initiated from the given bounded set BB in HH, which in turn shows that the set of all these vv-component functions are asymptotically compact in the space L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) by the compact embedding. Thus the proof is completed. ∎

Remark 2.

Remark 1 at the end of Section 4 said that the global attractor 𝒜\mathscr{A} for the Hindmarsh-Rose semiflow associated with the diffusive system (1.10) has a finite fractal dimension in HH via proof of the existence of an exponential attractor. It is a conjecture that the global attractors 𝒜1\mathscr{A}_{1} and 𝒜2\mathscr{A}_{2} for the partly diffusive Hindmarsh-Rose equations also have finite fractal dimensions in the space HH, but that is not pursued in this paper.
